name: Left
tagline: A stripped-down markdown writing app: local files, distraction-free typing, no workspace to log into.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A local markdown editor over a folder of plain text files is one of the most clonable products in software: CodeMirror plus a file watcher plus autosave gets you 80 percent of the feature list before lunch. The trouble is that the remaining 20 percent is the entire reason anyone pays for a writing app. Caret behaviour, scroll physics, undo granularity, how the app feels at 3000 words with the fan off, none of that shows up in a feature checklist and all of it takes months of fiddling. An agent will hand you something functional in one sitting, and you will notice the difference every time you type in it. Build it if you enjoy owning your tools, buy it if you actually want to write.
coreLoopDIY: Opens a folder of markdown files, lists them, edits them in a centred distraction-free pane, autosaves to disk, and renders a preview on demand.
requirements: a folder of markdown or text files
willingness to run an unsigned desktop build
whatYouLose: Native typing feel: cursor, scroll and undo behaviour that someone tuned for months
A signed, notarised app that opens instantly instead of an Electron shell
Any sync or mobile story at all, your notes live on one machine
Small conveniences you did not think to specify: smart lists, paste handling, link detection
Bug fixes and updates from someone who is not you
moatNotes: The moat is taste, not technology. Nothing here is hard to implement and everything here is hard to get right.
whyPeopleStillPay: Writing tools get judged on friction, and friction is invisible until it annoys you. People pay a small one-time price for an editor because they want to open it and start typing without noticing the software, and a self-built clone tends to draw attention to itself: a laggy keystroke, a scroll jump, an autosave that eats the last sentence. The DIY version is genuinely fine for notes and drafts. It is less fine as the place you go to write something long.
notes: Specifics here are drafted from the product's own framing rather than hands-on use, so treat the feature detail as unverified.
prompt:
Build a desktop markdown writing app for my own use. Local files only, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.

Stack, non negotiable: Electron with TypeScript, Vite for the renderer, CodeMirror 6 as the editor, marked for preview rendering, electron-store for settings, plain TS and CSS for the UI with no framework.

Behaviour:
- On first launch, ask for a folder. Remember it. That folder is the library, files are the source of truth, no database.
- Sidebar lists .md and .txt files sorted by modified time, with a filter box doing plain substring matching on filename and file contents.
- Main pane is a CodeMirror editor with markdown highlighting, soft wrap, and text capped around 68 characters wide and centred.
- Autosave to disk 400ms after the last keystroke. No save button. Never lose text, and reload from disk if a file changes externally while it is not focused.
- Cmd+N creates a file named from the first heading, slugified. Cmd+P quick open. Cmd+/ toggles a rendered preview pane. Cmd+Shift+F toggles focus mode, which dims every paragraph except the one holding the caret.
- Optional typewriter scrolling that keeps the caret vertically centred.
- Thin status bar with word count, character count and estimated reading time.
- Export the current file to HTML, and to PDF through the print dialog.
- Dark and light themes following the system setting, one accent colour, generous line height, a serif option and a mono option for the editor font.

Out of scope, do not build: sync, sharing, collaboration, plugins, image uploads, tags, backlinks, mobile, code signing, auto update, AI features.

One repo. README with dev and build commands. No .env needed because there are no secrets. It must work on first run with npm install then npm run dev, so do not leave placeholder functions.
